title: Faithful Messengers, Living Word
summary: Paul recalls the integrity and tenderness of the mission at Thessalonica, gives thanks for the word received amid persecution, and longs to see the church again.
historicalContext: Paul, Silas, and Timothy reached Thessalonica soon after Paul and Silas had been beaten with rods and jailed without trial at Philippi. For three Sabbaths Paul reasoned in the synagogue from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and some Jews, many God-fearing Greeks, and a number of leading women believed. Opponents then gathered a crowd from the marketplace, dragged Jason before the city magistrates, and charged the believers with loyalty to another king. The missionaries slipped away by night to Berea, and agitators pursued them there. In a busy port crowded with traveling orators, religious entrepreneurs, and teachers who lived off their hearers, such a hurried departure invited suspicion. Paul writes from Corinth, after Timothy’s return, to a young church still pressed by its own neighbors, recalling a ministry its members had watched at close range and could measure against the rumors circulating about it.
literaryContext: Chapter 2 expands two claims from chapter 1: that the gospel came through messengers whose manner of life the readers knew (1:5), and that others were reporting what kind of entrance the missionaries had (1:9). Verses 1–12 recall that visit through a chain of contrasts covering message, motive, and method, and through family images of an infant, a nursing mother, and a father. Verses 13–16 return to thanksgiving, tying the Thessalonians’ reception of the word to their suffering and setting their persecutors within a long biblical pattern of resistance to God’s messengers. Verses 17–20 open the account of separation that runs through 3:13, where the language of being orphaned, hindered by Satan, and longing for reunion turns toward the coming of the Lord Jesus. Throughout, Paul rests his case on what the readers themselves saw and remember.
themes: Holy conduct worthy of God’s kingdom
The word of God at work in believers
Suffering that joins churches across the world

outline.title: Boldness and Pure Motives
outline.summary: Paul recalls that the mission came with courage after Philippi, from motives tested by God and free of deceit, flattery, greed, or a craving for honor.

outline.title: Mother, Father, and Fellow Worker
outline.summary: The missionaries cared like a nursing mother, worked night and day, lived blamelessly, and urged each believer like a father to walk worthy of God.

outline.title: The Word Received Under Pressure
outline.summary: Paul thanks God that the church welcomed the message as God’s word and shared the sufferings of the Judean churches at the hands of opponents of the gospel.

outline.title: Separated in Body, Present in Heart
outline.summary: Torn away for a time and hindered by Satan, Paul longs to see the believers, whom he expects to rejoice over at the Lord’s coming.

verses.bibleText: For yourselves, brethren, know our entrance in unto you, that it was not in vain:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now turns from what others were reporting (1:9) to what the Thessalonians themselves knew. “For yourselves, brethren, know” sets the tone for the whole chapter: he will make no claim they cannot test against their own memory. The appeal suits a situation in which the missionaries had left suddenly and rumors were filling the silence. Rather than answering slander with counter-slander, Paul calls the church as witness to what it had seen.

“Entrance” refers to the visit itself, the arrival and the weeks of work that followed. Paul says it “was not in vain.” The underlying word means empty, and it can describe something hollow in content or barren in result. Both senses suit the defense that follows. The visit was no performance by men with nothing behind their words, and it was hardly fruitless, since the readers themselves were the fruit. A church that had turned from idols to serve the living God (1:9) was the evidence.

The address “brethren” belongs to the argument as well. Paul writes as one member of a family to others, and that family language will deepen through the chapter until he speaks of being orphaned by separation (v. 17). In his view a ministry is tested by what it produces in people and by the character of those who carry it, and both are open to inspection by those who received it.

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “a way in,” the noun denotes the missionaries’ arrival and reception in Thessalonica, including the whole founding visit. Paul uses the same word in 1:9, where others report what kind of welcome the preachers found. The term turns attention to the visit as an event the readers had witnessed for themselves.

The adjective means empty. It can describe words without substance or labor without result. Paul elsewhere fears that his work might prove empty if converts fall away, and he rejoices that God’s grace toward him was not empty. Here the denial covers both the integrity and the fruitfulness of the visit.

verses.bibleText: But even after that we had suffered before, and were shamefully entreated, as ye know, at Philippi, we were bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God with much contention.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul reminds the church of the circumstances in which the gospel reached them. Only days earlier he and Silas had been stripped, beaten with rods, and fastened in stocks at Philippi, all without a hearing and in spite of their Roman citizenship (Acts 16:22–24, 37). “Suffered before” recalls the pain; “shamefully entreated” recalls the public humiliation. In a culture that prized honor, such treatment was meant to discredit as much as to wound. Some in Thessalonica may still have seen the marks.

A man looking for easy profit would have taken that experience as a warning. Paul and his companions went on to the next city and spoke again. “We were bold” translates a verb associated with frank, open speech, the freedom to say what is true without hedging. Paul locates the source of that freedom “in our God.” The courage owed nothing to temperament. It came from the God whose message they carried and before whom they spoke.

The phrase “the gospel of God” appears three times in this chapter (vv. 2, 8, 9). The good news belongs to God; it originates with him and announces what he has done in his Son. The missionaries were its stewards, never its authors.

“With much contention” pictures a contest or struggle. The word could describe an athletic or legal contest, and here it covers the opposition the preachers met in Thessalonica, which ended in the uproar at Jason’s house (Acts 17:5–9). It may also include the inward strain of ministry under threat. Either way, the gospel arrived through people who had every human reason to stop. Their perseverance formed part of the evidence that their message did not rest on self-interest, and wherever believers keep speaking the truth at a cost, their steadiness often reaches observers before their arguments do.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb belongs to the family of parrēsia, open and fearless speech. In the Greek world it described a citizen’s freedom to speak plainly; in the New Testament it marks proclamation that does not shrink under threat. Paul qualifies it with “in our God,” grounding the boldness in God himself.

wordNotes.term: ἐν πολλῷ ἀγῶνι (en pollō agōni) — with much contention
wordNotes.explanation: Agōn denotes a contest or struggle, whether in the games, a courtroom, or battle. Paul uses it for the conflict that accompanies gospel work, both outward opposition and inward striving. It does not suggest that the preachers were quarrelsome; it describes the pressure under which they spoke.

verses.bibleText: For our exhortation was not of deceit, nor of uncleanness, nor in guile:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Verse 3 begins to explain that boldness. Paul calls his preaching “exhortation,” a word that combines appeal, encouragement, and comfort. The gospel came to the Thessalonians as an urgent invitation addressed to the heart as well as the mind, a message that pleads with hearers to be reconciled to God.

Three denials follow, and each seems to answer a charge easily made against wandering preachers. The appeal did not arise “of deceit,” that is, from error or delusion; the missionaries were not misled enthusiasts passing on a fantasy. Nor did it come “of uncleanness.” The word often refers to sexual impurity, and some cults of the day joined worship with immorality, so the denial may be quite literal. It can also cover impure motives more broadly, including greed. Finally, the message was not delivered “in guile,” with the bait-and-hook methods of a manipulator.

The three phrases move from the source of the message, to the motive of the messenger, to the method of delivery. Paul claims integrity at each level. The truth he preached was not invented, his heart was not ruled by appetite, and his manner was not calculated to trap.

These denials matter because the gospel cannot be separated from the character of those who carry it. A true message spread by deceptive means would contradict itself. Paul’s defense therefore serves the church more than himself. He wants them to know that what reached them was trustworthy from root to fruit, so that their faith could rest secure even while the messengers were absent and maligned.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun can mean appeal, encouragement, or consolation, depending on context. Here it names the apostolic preaching as a whole, a message that both summons and strengthens. The same root later describes how the missionaries dealt with each believer (2:11) and how the church should encourage one another (4:18).

wordNotes.term: πλάνη … ἀκαθαρσία … δόλος (planē … akatharsia … dolos) — deceit … uncleanness … guile
wordNotes.explanation: Planē is error or delusion, a wandering from the truth. Akatharsia is impurity, often sexual but sometimes extended to impure motives. Dolos is cunning, the trickery of bait used to catch prey. Together the three words deny any falsehood in the message, corruption in the motive, or manipulation in the method.

verses.bibleText: But as we were allowed of God to be put in trust with the gospel, even so we speak; not as pleasing men, but God, which trieth our hearts.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Over against those denials Paul sets the positive ground of his ministry: “as we were allowed of God to be put in trust with the gospel, even so we speak.” “Allowed” translates a verb meaning to test and approve, a word used for assaying metal. God had examined the missionaries and judged them fit to receive the gospel as a trust.

The image is that of a steward. A householder places property in the hands of a servant who must give account for it. Paul did not own the gospel or shape it to suit an audience. He held it on behalf of another, and what a master requires of a steward is faithfulness (1 Corinthians 4:1–2). What governed him was whether he had handed on the message intact.

“Not as pleasing men, but God.” Paul’s point concerns whose approval determines what is said. He was attentive to people, adapting his approach to Jews and Gentiles alike (1 Corinthians 9:19–22), and he could be gentle (v. 7). He would not trim the message to win applause. Anyone who lives for human approval must eventually choose between the audience and the truth.

The verse closes by returning to the verb of testing, now in the present tense: God “trieth our hearts.” The approval was no single past event that left Paul unaccountable afterward. God continues to examine the motives of his servants. Paul places himself under the searching gaze of the Lord who tests the heart (Jeremiah 17:10). That is sobering, and also freeing. A servant answerable to God need not be ruled by every rumor or criticism, because the final verdict on his ministry belongs to the One who sees what others cannot.

wordNotes.explanation: Paul uses the verb dokimazō twice, first in the perfect tense for God’s settled approval of the missionaries, then in the present tense for God’s continuing examination of their hearts. The word joins testing and approving: what has been tested is shown fit. The repetition frames the verse with divine scrutiny.

wordNotes.term: πιστευθῆναι τὸ εὐαγγέλιον (pisteuthēnai to euangelion) — to be put in trust with the gospel
wordNotes.explanation: The passive infinitive means to be entrusted. The gospel is pictured as a deposit placed in the hands of a steward who must guard it and deliver it faithfully. Paul speaks of his commission this way elsewhere, always as a gift received from God rather than a status he achieved.

verses.bibleText: For neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now becomes specific. “Neither at any time used we flattering words.” Flattery tells people what pleases them in order to gain something from them. It was a familiar vice among orators and teachers who depended on the goodwill of patrons and crowds. Had the missionaries flattered the Thessalonians, they would have left them comfortable in idolatry. The message instead called them to turn from idols (1:9), a summons no flatterer would issue.

“Nor a cloke of covetousness.” A cloak hides what lies underneath, and the word means a pretext, an outward show that conceals the true purpose. Paul denies that his preaching served as a respectable front for financial gain. He had taken nothing from them (v. 9), and he could later remind the Ephesian elders that he had coveted no one’s silver, gold, or clothing (Acts 20:33).

The two denials rest on different witnesses. On flattery Paul writes, “as ye know,” because speech can be heard and remembered. On covetousness he says, “God is witness,” because greed lives in the heart where only God sees. The appeal is solemn, close to an oath, and it shows a minister whose conscience lay open before God.

The verse exposes temptations that remain wherever spiritual influence can be turned into personal advantage. Praise can be used to manipulate, and religious language can mask a desire for money, comfort, or control. Paul’s answer is a life that can bear examination by people and by God at the same time.

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “a word of flattery,” the phrase describes speech shaped to please the hearer for the speaker’s gain. Moral teachers of the period often set the flatterer against the true friend who speaks frankly. The noun occurs only here in the New Testament, though the vice is condemned throughout Scripture.

wordNotes.term: προφάσει πλεονεξίας (prophasei pleonexias) — a cloke of covetousness
wordNotes.explanation: Prophasis is a pretext or pretense, an apparent reason used to cover the real one. Pleonexia is the desire to have more, especially at another’s expense. The phrase denies that religious activity served as a mask for greed.

verses.bibleText: Nor of men sought we glory, neither of you, nor yet of others, when we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
A third motive is set aside: the desire for honor. “Nor of men sought we glory, neither of you, nor yet of others.” In the Greco-Roman world reputation functioned as a kind of currency. Teachers competed for admirers, and public honor could open doors to patronage and influence. Paul does not say that no one ever honored him; he says that he did not pursue it, whether from the Thessalonians or from anyone else.

He adds that he could have acted differently: “when we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ.” The phrase can be read in two ways, and both may be present. It can refer to financial weight, the right of apostles to be supported by those they served (1 Corinthians 9:4–14). It can also refer to the weight of authority, the dignity with which an envoy of a king might carry himself and make demands. Paul possessed both rights and laid both aside.

The plural “apostles” deserves notice. Paul includes Silas and Timothy under the title, using it in the broader sense of commissioned messengers sent by Christ. Their authority came from the One who sent them, which is exactly why they had no need to inflate it.

Waiving a right can itself be a use of authority for the good of others. Christ, who shared the Father’s glory, emptied himself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:5–8). His messengers reflect him most clearly when they hold their position lightly for the sake of those they serve, and the church is strengthened by leaders who would sooner lose recognition than burden the people entrusted to them.

wordNotes.term: ἐν βάρει εἶναι (en barei einai) — to have been burdensome
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “to be in weight.” Baros can mean a burden laid on someone, such as financial demands, or weight in the sense of importance and authority. Paul likely plays on both: as Christ’s apostles the missionaries could have claimed support and asserted their dignity, yet they chose neither.

The word means those sent with a commission. Paul uses it here in a plural that includes Silas and Timothy, showing that the term could extend beyond the Twelve to other envoys of Christ. Their standing rested on Christ’s sending rather than on personal prominence.

verses.bibleText: But we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children.” After a string of denials Paul offers a portrait of what the missionaries were actually like. The contrast with verse 6 is sharp. Men who could have stood on their dignity behaved instead with tenderness.

A well-known textual question lies here. Many ancient manuscripts read nēpioi, “infants,” where others read ēpioi, “gentle.” The two words differ by a single letter, and the preceding Greek word ends with that same letter, which made confusion easy for copyists. If “infants” is original, Paul is saying that the missionaries were as guileless as little children, free of hidden schemes, before he turns to the image of a nursing mother. If “gentle” is original, as the KJV reads, the stress falls on kindness. Either reading points the same direction: the missionaries neither exploited their converts nor loomed over them, and the meaning of the passage does not hang on settling the question.

The second image is the more striking. “Nurse” translates a word for a woman who feeds an infant at the breast, whether a hired wet nurse or a mother. Paul specifies “her children,” her own, which suggests a mother nursing her own baby. The verb “cherisheth” means to warm or tend, and in the Greek Old Testament it describes a bird sheltering her young. Nothing in this picture involves calculation. The mother gives warmth, food, and attention without asking what the infant can contribute.

For a man of Paul’s training to describe his ministry with a maternal image shows how far he stood from the domineering leadership common in his world. Scripture itself speaks of God comforting his people as a mother comforts her child (Isaiah 66:13), and of a divine care more constant than a nursing mother’s (Isaiah 49:15). Paul’s gentleness reflected the character of the God he served. New believers, like newborns, need nourishment, protection, and patience, and those who lead them are called to supply it at their own expense.

wordNotes.explanation: The adjective means mild or kind and appears elsewhere in the New Testament only of the Lord’s servant, who must be gentle toward all. Many manuscripts read nēpioi, “infants,” a difference of one letter. The KJV follows “gentle.” Either way the emphasis falls on conduct free of harshness and hidden designs.

wordNotes.term: τροφὸς θάλπῃ (trophos thalpē) — a nurse cherisheth
wordNotes.explanation: Trophos is a nursing woman who feeds an infant. Thalpō means to warm, to cherish, to tend with care; the Greek Old Testament uses it of a mother bird sitting on her young, and Paul uses it again of the care a man gives his own body. The image is of nourishing, protective love.

verses.bibleText: So being affectionately desirous of you, we were willing to have imparted unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were dear unto us.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The maternal image continues. “So being affectionately desirous of you” uses a rare word for yearning, the warm attachment of a mother for her child. The missionaries did not merely tolerate their converts. They wanted them.

That longing produced a resolve: “we were willing to have imparted unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls.” “Willing” is better understood as “well pleased” or “glad.” Sharing their lives was something the missionaries delighted to do, never a burden grudgingly carried. The verb “imparted” means to share what one has with another, as a person gives part of his food or clothing to someone in need (Luke 3:11).

The word translated “souls” here means lives or selves. In Scripture the soul is the whole living person, not a detachable inner substance that outlasts the body by nature. Paul is saying that the missionaries gave themselves: their time, strength, safety, and affection. The gospel was not delivered at arm’s length. It came wrapped in the lives of those who brought it, who were ready even to risk death for the sake of their hearers.

The reason comes at the end: “because ye were dear unto us.” The Greek suggests “because you had become beloved.” Love had grown as the missionaries worked among the Thessalonians, prayed for them, and watched them stand under pressure.

This verse holds truth and love together in a way every form of Christian witness needs. The message is God’s and must be delivered faithfully, yet a message passed along without self-giving contradicts the gospel it describes. Christ gave himself for those he loved (Galatians 2:20), and his messengers follow him when they offer the same.

wordNotes.explanation: This rare verb, found only here in the New Testament, expresses yearning or tender longing. It belongs to the vocabulary of affection rather than duty. Paul uses it to describe a warm attachment that issues in self-giving, much as he elsewhere speaks of longing for believers with the tender mercies of Christ.

Psychē here means life or self, the whole person in living existence. Paul is speaking of giving one’s very life and energies, not of an immortal inner part separable from the body. Jesus uses the same word when he speaks of the good shepherd laying down his life for the sheep.

verses.bibleText: For ye remember, brethren, our labour and travail: for labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you, we preached unto you the gospel of God.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul supports his claim of self-giving love with a concrete memory: “ye remember, brethren, our labour and travail.” The two nouns are paired elsewhere in his letters for exhausting work and hardship (2 Corinthians 11:27; 2 Thessalonians 3:8). The Thessalonians had watched it happen.

“Labouring night and day” describes Paul’s trade. Acts identifies him as a tentmaker, a craftsman in cloth or leather (Acts 18:3), and the ancient workday began before dawn. Paul seems to have worked long hours at his bench and preached in whatever time remained, perhaps conversing with customers and fellow workers in the shop itself. Many in the upper classes looked down on manual labor, and a teacher who worked with his hands surrendered social standing. Paul accepted that loss.

His purpose was clear: “because we would not be chargeable unto any of you.” As an apostle he had a right to support (1 Corinthians 9:14), and he gladly received gifts from the Philippians, sent to him more than once while he was in Thessalonica (Philippians 4:16). Still, he would not lay a financial weight on new believers who were themselves largely working people, and he would give no one grounds to say that the gospel was a business.

“We preached unto you the gospel of God.” The verb is that of a herald announcing a royal message. The free gift of God was offered freely.

The verse honors ordinary work as a setting for faithful witness, and it warns against anything that makes the gospel look like a product for sale. Paul later held up his own labor as a pattern for believers who had stopped working (2 Thessalonians 3:7–9), showing that diligence and devotion belong together.

wordNotes.term: κόπον καὶ μόχθον (kopon kai mochthon) — labour and travail
wordNotes.explanation: Kopos is toil to the point of weariness; mochthos adds the idea of hardship and struggle. Paired together the words describe exhausting work under difficult conditions. Paul uses the same pair for his apostolic hardships and for his self-supporting labor in Thessalonica.

The verb means to weigh down or impose a burden. Paul uses it for financial dependence that would burden his converts. It echoes the “weight” of verse 6 and shows that his refusal to be a burden was a deliberate policy, one he maintained in other churches as well.

verses.bibleText: Ye are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly and unblameably we behaved ourselves among you that believe:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul summons two witnesses: “Ye are witnesses, and God also.” The church could testify to what it saw; God could testify to what lay beneath. A claim made before both is a claim made with full seriousness.

Three adverbs describe the missionaries’ conduct. “Holily” points to devotion toward God, a life that honors what God regards as sacred. “Justly” points to uprightness, especially in dealings with others. “Unblameably” means that no charge could rightly stick. Together they describe a life rightly ordered toward God and neighbor, with nothing left for a fair accuser to seize.

The phrase “among you that believe” may mean that the believers saw this conduct most closely, or that it was offered for their benefit. Either way, the testimony comes from people who had observed the missionaries in the workshop, the synagogue, and their own homes.

Paul is not claiming sinless perfection. He is claiming an integrity of life that matched the message. Later in the letter he prays that the Thessalonians themselves will be established “unblameable in holiness” at Christ’s coming (3:13). What he asks for them he first demonstrated before them, and those who teach always teach by example as well as by word.

wordNotes.term: ὁσίως καὶ δικαίως καὶ ἀμέμπτως (hosiōs kai dikaiōs kai amemptōs) — holily and justly and unblameably
wordNotes.explanation: The first adverb concerns piety toward God, the second righteous conduct toward people, and the third freedom from any justified accusation. Paul uses related words when he speaks of believers being preserved blameless for Christ’s coming, so his description of the missionaries anticipates his prayer for the church.

verses.bibleText: As ye know how we exhorted and comforted and charged every one of you, as a father doth his children,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Having likened the missionaries to a nursing mother, Paul adds a second family image: “as a father doth his children.” In the ancient household the father bore responsibility for training children in character and conduct, and Paul’s three verbs describe that role.

They “exhorted,” urging the believers forward in the faith. They “comforted,” speaking encouragement to those weighed down by grief or fear. They “charged,” testifying solemnly to what God requires, like a witness under oath. Taken together the verbs show pastoral care that was neither merely soft nor merely severe. Encouragement, consolation, and earnest warning each had a place, according to the need of the person.

“Every one of you” is significant. Paul did not speak only to crowds. He dealt with individuals, knew their struggles, and fitted his counsel to each. Such personal attention suited the setting of the mission, in which much teaching probably took place in homes and workshops.

The pairing of mother and father completes Paul’s picture of ministry. The mother nourishes and protects; the father guides and instructs. Both images are rooted in love, and both aim at the child’s maturity. Those who care for others in the faith need both qualities: a tenderness that makes people feel safe, and a firmness that helps them grow.

wordNotes.term: παρακαλοῦντες καὶ παραμυθούμενοι καὶ μαρτυρόμενοι (parakalountes kai paramythoumenoi kai martyromenoi) — exhorted and comforted and charged
wordNotes.explanation: The first participle means to urge or appeal; the second to console or encourage, especially the discouraged; the third to testify solemnly, insisting on what is required. Paul uses the second verb again when he tells the church to comfort the fainthearted.

verses.bibleText: That ye would walk worthy of God, who hath called you unto his kingdom and glory.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The goal of all this exhorting and comforting is now stated: “That ye would walk worthy of God.” “Walk” is a common biblical image for the whole course of a person’s conduct, taken step by step. To walk worthy of God is to live in a way that fits who God is and what he has done. The standard is high, yet the phrase speaks of fitting response, not of earning. People do not become worthy of God by their walk; they are summoned to a walk that corresponds to the God who has called them.

That call is expressed in the present tense in the best-attested text: God is the one “who calls you,” not merely one who called once long ago. His summons keeps sounding through the word and drawing believers on. The call is “unto his kingdom and glory.” God’s kingdom is already present as his reign of grace in those who receive him (Colossians 1:13). It will be fully revealed when Christ returns and his people enter the kingdom of glory (Matthew 25:31–34). Paul’s phrase holds both together. The Thessalonians already belonged to God’s kingdom, and they were moving toward its consummation.

“Glory” points to the splendor of God’s own presence, which his people will share at the end. Believers will appear with Christ in glory when he appears (Colossians 3:4).

The verse displays the shape of the Christian life. God takes the initiative, calling people to himself, and those who hear respond with lives that reflect his character. How believers live now is the visible sign that they belong to the coming kingdom. Paul returns to the theme in chapter 4, where he urges the church to walk so as to please God and to abound more and more. Grace that calls also produces obedience.

wordNotes.term: περιπατεῖν … ἀξίως τοῦ θεοῦ (peripatein … axiōs tou theou) — walk worthy of God
wordNotes.explanation: Peripateō, literally to walk about, is a regular Pauline image for daily conduct, drawn from Hebrew idiom. Axiōs means in a fitting or befitting manner. The phrase does not describe merit that earns God’s favor; it describes a life that corresponds to God’s character and call.

wordNotes.term: τοῦ καλοῦντος (tou kalountos) — who hath called
wordNotes.explanation: The best-attested reading is a present participle, “who calls,” stressing that God’s summons is ongoing. Some manuscripts have the aorist, which the KJV renders “hath called.” Either way, the call originates with God and draws believers into his kingdom and glory.

verses.bibleText: For this cause also thank we God without ceasing, because, when ye received the word of God which ye heard of us, ye received it not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God, which effectually worketh also in you that believe.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For this cause also thank we God without ceasing.” Paul returns to the thanksgiving of 1:2, now with a specific reason. Having described how the missionaries brought the message, he turns to how the Thessalonians received it.

Two different Greek verbs stand behind the twice-repeated “received.” The first means to take over something handed on, the reception of a message heard. The second means to welcome, to accept inwardly. The Thessalonians did more than hear a report; they embraced what they heard. And they welcomed it “not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God.”

This is a remarkable claim about apostolic preaching. Paul did not regard his message as religious opinion or the product of his own reflection. It came from God, and the Thessalonians rightly recognized it as such. Paul had reasoned with them from the Scriptures, showing from the Old Testament that the Messiah had to suffer and rise (Acts 17:2–3), so the gospel he preached stood in continuity with the written word God had already given. The phrase “as it is in truth” insists that the message is God’s word whatever anyone makes of it; the Thessalonians simply perceived what it really was.

The verse then describes what the word does: it “effectually worketh also in you that believe.” The verb speaks of energy at work, power producing effects. God’s word is far from inert information. It changes those who receive it, producing faith, love, and hope (1:3), turning people from idols (1:9), and sustaining them in suffering (v. 14). It accomplishes what God sends it to do (Isaiah 55:11).

Yet the word works “in you that believe.” Faith is the channel through which its power operates, and the same message heard by an unbelieving heart may change nothing (Hebrews 4:2). The verse therefore joins God’s initiative and human response: the power belongs to God’s word, and it is received by faith. Whenever Scripture is read and heard with trust, that same power is active. The church should handle it with the reverence due to the voice of God and expect it to reshape those who welcome it.

wordNotes.explanation: The first verb, paralambanō, is used for receiving a tradition handed on, the outward hearing of the message. The second, dechomai, means to welcome or accept, often with the warmth of hospitality. Paul distinguishes hearing the gospel from embracing it and rejoices that the Thessalonians did both.

The verb means to be at work, to be operative and effective. Paul uses this word family for the power of God active in believers. Here the subject is the word of God, which keeps working in those who believe and produces the transformation described in chapter 1.

verses.bibleText: For ye, brethren, became followers of the churches of God which in Judaea are in Christ Jesus: for ye also have suffered like things of your own countrymen, even as they have of the Jews:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Verse 14 offers evidence that the word was truly at work: the Thessalonians had suffered for it and stood firm. “Ye, brethren, became followers of the churches of God which in Judaea are in Christ Jesus.” The word “followers” means imitators. The Thessalonians had not deliberately copied the Judean believers, but their experience had come to match it. Faithfulness under persecution placed them in the same company.

The phrase “in Christ Jesus” marks these Judean congregations plainly as Christian churches. They were largely Jewish believers who had been the first to suffer for confessing Jesus as Messiah (Acts 8:1–3; 12:1–3). Paul himself had once been among their persecutors (Galatians 1:22–23). To be linked with them was an honor for a young Gentile church.

“Ye also have suffered like things of your own countrymen.” The word means fellow citizens, people of the same locality. In Thessalonica the trouble was stirred up by some members of the synagogue, but it was carried out by a mob gathered from the marketplace and brought before the city authorities (Acts 17:5–9). The Thessalonians’ persecutors were mostly their own Gentile neighbors. Paul’s comparison runs between two churches, each suffering at the hands of people from its own community.

“Even as they have of the Jews.” In this setting the term refers to those in Judea who opposed the Judean churches, especially the leaders who used their power against the followers of Jesus. The Judean believers were themselves Jews; the conflict Paul describes took place within one people, between those who received Jesus as Messiah and those who violently resisted that confession. This distinction is essential for reading the verses that follow.

For the Thessalonians the comfort was that suffering did not mean they had gone astray. It joined them to the experience of God’s people elsewhere and, as the next verse shows, to the experience of the prophets and of the Lord himself.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun means imitators. In 1:6 Paul uses it of the Thessalonians’ imitation of the missionaries and of the Lord. Here the imitation is a likeness of experience: by suffering for the gospel, the church came to resemble the believers of Judea. The term implies shared identity as well as copying.

wordNotes.term: τῶν Ἰουδαίων (tōn Ioudaiōn) — of the Jews
wordNotes.explanation: Ioudaioi can mean Jews generally, Judeans, or in some contexts the Jewish authorities. Here the setting limits it to those in Judea who persecuted the Judean churches. Since those churches were themselves Jewish, the word cannot mean the Jewish people as a whole; it names particular opponents of the gospel.

verses.bibleText: Who both killed the Lord Jesus, and their own prophets, and have persecuted us; and they please not God, and are contrary to all men:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now describes those who opposed the Judean churches. The KJV punctuation, “of the Jews: Who both killed…,” can make the description sound like a statement about Jews as a whole. The context points elsewhere. Paul is speaking of the particular opponents named at the end of verse 14, the persecutors of the Judean believers, and he lists their actions to show the pattern into which the Thessalonians’ suffering fits. Paul himself was a Jew who could wish himself accursed for the sake of his kinsmen (Romans 9:3), and he later insisted that God has not cast away his people (Romans 11:1–2). These verses are a prophetic indictment of persecution, of the same kind Israel’s own prophets and Jesus himself pronounced. Christians have at times twisted them into a warrant for contempt or cruelty toward Jewish people, and that is a grave misuse of Scripture.

“Who both killed the Lord Jesus.” The Gospels and Acts describe how leaders in Jerusalem handed Jesus over to Roman authority to be crucified (Acts 2:23; 3:13–15). Yet the New Testament also gathers Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel together in that act (Acts 4:27), and it teaches that Christ died for the sins of all. No group may point to another as uniquely guilty, since every sinner stands in need of the same cross.

“And their own prophets.” The phrase draws on the long biblical record of prophets rejected and slain by those they warned (1 Kings 19:10; Nehemiah 9:26). Jesus spoke of Jerusalem as the city that killed the prophets (Matthew 23:37), and Paul sets the persecution of Christ’s messengers in that same line.

“And have persecuted us.” The verb suggests being driven out, most likely a reference to the way the missionaries were forced from Thessalonica and then from Berea (Acts 17:5–10, 13).

“And they please not God.” This stands over against verse 4. Paul sought to please God; these opponents, for all their zeal, did not (Romans 10:2). “And are contrary to all men.” Paul is not describing general unfriendliness, and the next verse explains what he does mean: by opposing the gospel to the Gentiles, they set themselves against the good of all humanity. The charge concerns resistance to God’s saving purpose, and it falls on anyone, of any nation, who tries to block it.

wordNotes.explanation: This compound verb occurs only here in the New Testament. The prefix likely gives the sense “to drive out” or “to chase away,” and the aorist tense points to a specific event. It fits the forced departure of the missionaries from Thessalonica described in Acts and recalled in 2:17.

wordNotes.term: θεῷ μὴ ἀρεσκόντων (theō mē areskontōn) — please not God
wordNotes.explanation: Pleasing God is one of Paul’s chief ways of describing faithful living. He has just claimed it for the missionaries (2:4) and will urge it on the church (4:1). Applied to persecutors of the gospel, the phrase means that their zeal ran against God’s purpose, however sincere it may have felt.

verses.bibleText: Forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles that they might be saved, to fill up their sins alway: for the wrath is come upon them to the uttermost.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Verse 16 explains how these opponents were “contrary to all men”: they were “forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles that they might be saved.” The hostility Paul describes was aimed at the spread of the gospel. In Acts, opposition followed the missionaries from city to city, often provoked because salvation through Jesus was being offered to Gentiles on equal terms (Acts 13:45–50; 22:21–22). To obstruct that message was to stand in the way of the salvation God intends for the nations. For Paul nothing could be more serious, because the gospel is God’s power to save everyone who believes (Romans 1:16).

The outcome of such resistance is that they “fill up their sins alway.” The image is of a measure being filled until it brims over. God told Abraham that the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full (Genesis 15:16), and Jesus told the scribes and Pharisees who opposed him to fill up the measure of their fathers (Matthew 23:32). God is patient and long-suffering, but persistent rejection of light accumulates until judgment can no longer be delayed. “Alway” suggests a pattern stretching through history, from the rejection of the prophets to the opposition Paul faced.

“For the wrath is come upon them to the uttermost.” The verb is past tense, yet the full outpouring of judgment still lay ahead. Paul may be speaking with prophetic certainty of what was already decided, much as Jesus had foretold the destruction of Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–44; 21:20–24), which came in A.D. 70. He may also mean that the wrath had already begun to fall in the hardening and calamities of his own day. The phrase “to the uttermost” can mean fully, at last, or until the end.

What the verse leaves unsaid is equally important. It does not pronounce a final verdict on every Jewish person or close the door of mercy. In Romans 11 Paul speaks of a remnant chosen by grace, of broken branches that can be grafted in again, and of God’s gifts and calling as irrevocable (Romans 11:5, 23, 29). The warning applies to all who persist in resisting God’s message, whoever they are. For the Thessalonians the point was reassurance: those who opposed them were not beyond God’s notice, and judgment belonged to him, not to the persecuted.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to fill to completion. Biblical writers use the image of a measure of sin that grows until judgment falls, as with the Amorites and with those Jesus rebuked. The image stresses both divine patience and the accountability that follows persistent resistance to God’s word.

wordNotes.term: εἰς τέλος (eis telos) — to the uttermost
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase can mean “fully,” “at last,” or “until the end.” The KJV takes it in the sense of completeness. Read alongside Paul’s hope for Israel in Romans 11, the expression conveys the seriousness and certainty of judgment on persistent opposition without declaring every member of a people beyond God’s mercy.

verses.bibleText: But we, brethren, being taken from you for a short time in presence, not in heart, endeavoured the more abundantly to see your face with great desire.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul turns from the opponents back to the church, and his tone becomes intensely personal. “But we, brethren, being taken from you for a short time in presence, not in heart.” The verb behind “being taken from you” is built on the word for an orphan. Paul has already pictured himself as an infant, a nursing mother, and a father; now he describes the separation as a bereavement within a family. The departure from Thessalonica had been forced, sudden, and painful (Acts 17:10).

“For a short time” is literally “for the season of an hour.” Paul may mean that the separation was meant to be brief, or that it had begun only recently. Either way it was unchosen, and he did not regard it as permanent. “In presence, not in heart” draws the line between physical absence and inward attachment. Distance had changed where he was, not whom he loved.

The rest of the verse piles up words of intensity: they “endeavoured the more abundantly to see your face with great desire.” Separation had sharpened his longing instead of dulling it. Opponents may have claimed that Paul had run away and forgotten his converts, and his words meet that suspicion head-on. The missionaries had made every effort to return.

The verse reveals how Paul understood the church: as a family whose bonds survive distance, and whose members feel separation as loss. Fellowship in Christ is more than shared opinion. It is a belonging that longs to be together and counts reunion as one of its joys.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb, found only here in the New Testament, is built on the word for orphan. It describes being bereaved or forcibly separated. Whether Paul pictures himself as an orphaned child or as a parent bereft of children, the image conveys the pain of a family torn apart.

wordNotes.term: πρὸς καιρὸν ὥρας (pros kairon hōras) — for a short time
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “for a season of an hour,” an idiom for a brief period. Paul stresses that the separation was meant to be temporary, though it had already lasted longer than he wished. The phrase carries both his hope of return and his frustration at the delay.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore we would have come unto you, even I Paul, once and again; but Satan hindered us.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Wherefore we would have come unto you, even I Paul, once and again.” Paul steps briefly out of the plural he uses through most of the letter to speak for himself. Silas and Timothy shared the desire, but Paul wants the church to know that he personally had tried more than once to return. “Once and again” is an idiom for repeated attempts.

“But Satan hindered us.” The verb was used of breaking up a road to stop an army’s advance, or of cutting in on a runner in a race. Paul does not say what form the obstacle took. It may have been the security Jason had been forced to post (Acts 17:9), continuing danger in the city, illness, or some other circumstance. What matters is how Paul reads it. Behind the obstacle he sees the work of the adversary who opposes the gospel.

This is significant because Paul elsewhere credits changes in his travel plans to the Holy Spirit (Acts 16:6–7). He did not treat every closed door as satanic. Here, however, he discerned that the barrier came from the enemy’s opposition, not from God’s guidance. Scripture presents the conflict between Christ and Satan as real and ongoing, with Satan working to obstruct God’s work and harm God’s people (Ephesians 6:12; Revelation 12:17). Daniel was told that a heavenly messenger sent in answer to his prayer had been withstood for three weeks (Daniel 10:12–13).

Yet Satan’s power is limited. He could delay Paul’s return, but he could not undo the work of the word in Thessalonica. Paul sent Timothy instead (3:1–2), and he wrote this letter, which has strengthened believers ever since. The hindrance became an occasion for wider ministry. Believers today may face obstacles they cannot explain, and they need discernment to distinguish God’s redirection from the enemy’s resistance. In either case they can rest on the victory Christ has already won, knowing that the adversary’s schemes will not have the final word.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to cut into, and it was used of obstructing a road or cutting in on a runner. Paul applies it to obstacles that blocked his way. The New Testament also uses it for whatever impedes believers in their course or in their prayers.

The name comes from a Hebrew word meaning adversary or accuser. In Scripture Satan is a personal being who opposes God and his people, tempts them, and seeks to obstruct the gospel. Paul calls him “the tempter” in 3:5. His power is real but limited, and God has promised to crush him.

verses.bibleText: For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing? Are not even ye in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now explains why he longed so earnestly to return: “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing?” He answers with another question: “Are not even ye in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming?” The Thessalonians themselves were what Paul hoped to see, rejoice over, and glory in on that day.

The “crown” here is the wreath awarded to a victor in the games or bestowed to honor a citizen for public service. “Crown of rejoicing” is literally “crown of boasting.” Paul is not boasting in his own achievement; he glories in what God has done through him (Romans 15:17–18; 1 Corinthians 15:10). The Thessalonians are evidence of God’s grace, and Paul looks forward to presenting them to Christ as the fruit of his labor.

The setting of this hope is “in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming.” The word “coming,” parousia, was used for the official visit of a ruler to a city, an arrival welcomed with public celebration. It becomes a key word in the Thessalonian letters (3:13; 4:15; 5:23). Christ’s coming will be personal, visible, and public. Paul does not place his reunion with his converts at the moment of death; he places it at Christ’s return, when the dead in Christ will be raised and the living changed (4:16–17). That is when the faithful will stand before the Lord together.

This hope shapes Paul’s ministry. He measures success by whether those he served will stand in Christ’s presence on that day, and numbers or reputation count for little beside it. Every relationship formed in the gospel looks forward to that meeting, and anyone who serves others may ask whether the people they have influenced will be found faithful when the Lord appears.

wordNotes.term: στέφανος καυχήσεως (stephanos kauchēseōs) — crown of rejoicing
wordNotes.explanation: Stephanos was the victor’s wreath in athletic contests or a garland of honor. Kauchēsis is boasting or glorying, which Paul treats positively when its ground is God’s work. The phrase pictures the Thessalonians as Paul’s prize and cause for joy before Christ.

The word means presence or arrival, and it was used for the visit of a king or high official to a city. In the New Testament it refers to the personal, visible return of Christ. Paul uses it repeatedly in these letters for the event at which the dead are raised and believers are gathered to the Lord.

verses.bibleText: For ye are our glory and joy.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For ye are our glory and joy.” Paul answers his own question with an emphatic affirmation. The pronoun stands first in the Greek: it is “you” who are his glory and joy. Verse 19 looked ahead to the day of Christ’s coming; verse 20 states what is already true. The Thessalonians were his glory and joy now, and they would be then.

“Glory” here means honor, the thing in which a person takes pride. Paul’s honor lay outside status, wealth, or reputation, which he had renounced (vv. 5–6). It was found in people who had turned to God and stood firm in faith. “Joy” is the delight of seeing God at work in others.

The short verse closes the chapter with warmth. After defending his conduct, giving thanks for their faith, and voicing his longing to see them, Paul assures the church that they hold a central place in his heart. The words also prepare for chapter 3, where Timothy’s good report brings relief and renewed joy (3:6–9). The reward Paul looked for was other people standing firm in Christ.

wordNotes.term: ἡ δόξα ἡμῶν καὶ ἡ χαρά (hē doxa hēmōn kai hē chara) — our glory and joy
wordNotes.explanation: Doxa here means honor or that in which one glories; chara is joy or delight. Paul gives both titles to the church itself, showing that his reward lay in people and not in prestige. The same pairing of joy and glorying in converts appears in his letter to Philippi.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: If people watched your daily conduct closely for several weeks, what would they conclude about the motives behind your faith?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God’s word is carried most credibly by messengers who seek God’s approval, give themselves for others, and hold fast amid opposition while looking toward Christ’s coming.
discussionQuestions: Why does Paul appeal so often to what the Thessalonians themselves saw and remember?
How do the images of a nursing mother and a father together describe faithful Christian leadership?
What is the difference between hearing a message and receiving it as the word of God?
How should verses 14–16 be read so that they warn against resisting the gospel without fostering contempt for any people?
Why does Paul measure his joy by the believers he hopes to see at Christ’s coming?
commonMisunderstandings: Refusing to please people is no license for harshness; the same passage describes Paul as gentle as a nursing mother.
Verses 14–16 do not condemn the Jewish people as a whole; Paul, the Judean believers, and Jesus himself were Jews, and Paul speaks of particular opponents of the gospel.
Walking worthy of God does not earn the kingdom; it is the fitting response to the God who calls.
Satan’s hindrance does not mean God’s purposes have failed, nor that every obstacle is demonic.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep message and messenger together: the gospel Paul preached was matched by a life that commended it, and the same word now works in those who believe.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Receive God’s word as his own voice, let it reshape your motives and your care for others, and live now in view of the day you will stand before the Lord Jesus at his coming.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: The gospel is God’s own word, received by faith and powerfully at work in believers, calling them into his present kingdom of grace and his coming glory.
flow: The gospel originates with God, not with human cleverness or ambition.
God entrusts this message to messengers whose lives are open to examination.
When the message is welcomed as God’s word, it begins to work in the one who believes.
God calls those who receive it into his kingdom now and his glory at Christ’s return.
That call produces a life worthy of God, sustained even under pressure.
simpleIllustrations: A letter from a trusted parent is read differently from an advertisement; the Thessalonians heard the gospel as a message from God himself.
A mother nursing her baby keeps no account of what the child owes her; the missionaries gave themselves with the same unpaid love.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you receive the message of Christ as the word of God and let it begin its work in your life today?
cautions: Do not use verses 14–16 to cast blame on Jewish people; present the warning as one against resisting God’s messengers wherever it occurs.
Do not make the preacher’s sincerity the ground of faith; the power lies in the word of God itself.
Do not treat suffering as evidence of God’s disfavor; Paul presents it as the shared path of faithful churches.

reflectionQuestions: Whose approval most shapes what I say and do when I speak about my faith?
Where am I tempted to use flattery, image, or advantage in place of plain truth and love?
Who has shared not only the gospel but their own life with me, and with whom am I doing the same?
Do I treat Scripture as human opinion to be weighed, or as the word of God to be welcomed and obeyed?
Whom do I hope to see rejoicing with me at the coming of Jesus?
